abstract: We propose novel approachs to information transmission in scattering media such as multimode fibers (MMF). By utilizing the physical basis of the model, training with pure eigenmode data enables precise mode decomposition, which is of great importance in high-rate secure multimode fiber communication. In this work, we present physics-based deep learning methods for the mode demultiplexing (MD) of MMF. The "Physics-in-Loss" method utilizes the physical premise that an MMF represents the linear superposition of its eigenmodes. This eliminates the need for large datasets and lengthy training sessions. MD of over 5,000 modes is achieved. However, mainly we focus on "Physics-in-Network" which is based on optical diffractive neural networks. It operates with minimal energy consumption and very low latency. For real-time mode demultiplexing, training with only eigenmode distributions is sufficient to achieve precise results. We will highlight the unique advantages, trade-offs and applications to information transmission via scattering media.
title: Physics-informed deep learning with optical neural networks for information transmission through scattering media

abstract: We present a scalable neuromorphic photonic computing architecture based on a χ⁽³⁾ silicon nitride waveguide. Using three-dimensional FDTD simulation, we characterize nonlinear mode coupling across 15 guided modes and verify linear scaling of the nonlinear field difference across four propagation lengths — 12.5, 25, 50, and 100 micrometers — confirming Kerr nonlinear accumulation consistent with theory. Simulation cost is minimized through length-nonlinearity equivalence scaling, reducing all production runs to the 12.5 μm geometry. A dataset of input mode combinations and corresponding output mode coefficients — extracted via modal decomposition at the output facet — trains a neural network surrogate that replaces expensive FDTD evaluations during optimization. The S-matrix formalism describes the inverse design region, enabling gradient-based joint optimization of input modes and waveguide geometry. Each waveguide-plus-inverse-design pair acts as a cascadable physical neural network layer, forming a scalable architecture for mode conversion, multiplexing, and neuromorphic optical computing.
title: Scalable neuromorphic photonic architecture based on nonlinear Si₃N₄ waveguides and neural network surrogate modeling

abstract: The realization of ultrafast, low-power optical neural networks requires physically embedded nonlinear activation mechanisms compatible with Fourier-based photonic architectures. We demonstrate a convolutional optical neural network (OCNN) driven by a femtosecond-pulsed telecom laser, enabling intrinsic nonlinear activation via material absorption rather than electronic post-processing. Convolution is implemented in the Fourier plane using a spatial light modulator (SLM), with Laguerre-Gaussian modes serving as an orthogonal kernel basis. Object information is encoded directly onto the beam and processed through parallel Fourier-domain filtering. Nonlinear activation arises from two-photon absorption (TPA) in a CMOS camera, providing an intensity-dependent response without external electronic nonlinearities while remaining compatible with telecom wavelengths. The high peak intensities of ultrashort pulses enable scalable nonlinear activation at low average power. In object classification tasks, we achieve >90% accuracy, comparable to state-of-the-art OCNNs, establishing a pathway toward scalable, all-optical neuromorphic processors.
title: Toward scalable nonlinearities in convolutional optical neural networks driven by ultrashort laser pulses

abstract: Matrix–matrix multiplication (MMM) is the dominant computational primitive in modern deep-learning workloads, and its electronic implementation is increasingly bounded by the energy and interconnect limits of CMOS. Existing photonic accelerators largely perform only matrix–vector multiplication or operate at limited scale. We present a free-space photonic MMM architecture that combines two thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) phase-only spatial light modulators (SLMs) in a 4-f Fourier relay to perform true C=A⋅B in the outer-product, time-integrating regime of Athale and Collins [ Appl. Opt. 21 , 2089 ( 1982 ). APOPAI 0003-6935 10.1364/AO.21.002089 ], replacing kilohertz-rate liquid-crystal or acousto-optic modulation with gigahertz-rate electro-optic phase modulation. The outer product is formed by cascading a row-encoded and a column-encoded amplitude mask in an imaging relay; the Fourier shift theorem is used to place the amplitude-carrying diffraction order of each phase-only SLM in a Fourier-plane spatial filter. We derive the architecture from first principles and validate it with a three-layer physical simulation: scalar-diffraction modeling of the pixelated SLMs and 4-f relay, a full detector-noise Monte Carlo of the time-integrating accumulation, and end-to-end neural-network inference executed entirely through the physical model. Carrier-order placement is accurate to 0.09% of the row pitch with an 8-bit phase DAC; at the nominal 100 mW design point, the simulated processor achieves 6.4 effective bits at N=128 under a conservative 100 ps photon-integration window (about 8 bits when photons are integrated over the full 1 ns cycle), shot-noise limited, and 95.8% classification accuracy on a handwritten-digit benchmark versus 98.3% for float32 and INT8 digital execution. We quantify the effect of inter-pixel phase blur on the phase-only amplitude encoding end-to-end, showing that a two-level checkerboard with a blur of 0.1 pixel pitch limits the usable matrix dimension to N≈64 unless guard rows are added between macropixels, give a full-latency (compute plus readout) throughput and energy accounting, and break down the assumed optical efficiency and the physical volume. For N=1024, the compute subsystem projects 2 PFLOPS at sub-10 fJ/MAC; including detector readout with a pipelined read-out integrated circuit and a deep inner dimension, the full-latency figures are 1.7 PFLOPS at ≈9fJ/MAC, and the simulation quantifies the optical power (≈0.6−6W, depending on the integration window) required to reach INT8 precision at that scale.
title: Gigahertz thin-film lithium niobate phase-SLM architecture for true matrix–matrix multiplication in photonic AI accelerators: design and physical-layer simulation
